title: Erdős Problem #400: Factorial Divisibility and Sum Excess
description: For k ≥ 2, let g_k(n) = max{(a₁+⋯+aₖ)-n : a₁!⋯aₖ! | n!}. Is Σ g_k(n) ~ cₖ·x·log x? Is g_k(n) concentrated around cₖ·log x?

meta.author: Erdős, Graham (1980)
originalContributions: Defined FactorialDivides for the product divisibility condition
Defined sumExcess and gExcess (g_k(n)) as the supremum of sum excesses
Axiomatized the Erdős-Graham upper bound g_k(n) = O(log n)
Developed the k = 2 case with binomial coefficient connection

overview.historicalContext:
Erdős and Graham studied this problem in their 1980 monograph [ErGr80, p. 77], investigating the maximum excess that k factorials can achieve over n! while dividing it. The function g_k(n) measures the maximum amount by which the sum a₁ + ⋯ + aₖ can exceed n, subject to the constraint that the product a₁!⋯aₖ! divides n!. This is a natural question about the divisibility structure of factorials.

Erdős and Graham established the fundamental bound g_k(n) = O(log n), showing that the excess grows at most logarithmically. This is because the condition a₁!⋯aₖ! | n! is equivalent to saying that n!/(a₁!⋯aₖ!) is an integer — a multinomial coefficient — and the logarithmic bound follows from analyzing the prime factorization constraints. The precise asymptotics, however, remain unknown.

The problem has two parts: (a) whether the average value of g_k(n) for n ≤ x grows like cₖ·x·log x for some constant cₖ depending on k, and (b) whether g_k(n) is concentrated around cₖ·log x for almost all n ≤ x. For the special case k = 2, the condition a!·b! | n! means that the binomial coefficient C(n, a) is an integer (which it always is), so the problem reduces to maximizing a + b - n subject to a + b ≤ 2n.
overview.problemStatement: For $k \ge 2$, let $g_k(n) = \max\{(a_1 + \cdots + a_k) - n : a_1! \cdots a_k! \mid n!\}$. (a) Is $\sum_{n \le x} g_k(n) \sim c_k \cdot x \cdot \log x$? (b) Is $g_k(n) = c_k \cdot \log x + o(\log x)$ for almost all $n \le x$?
overview.proofStrategy: We define FactorialDivides (the divisibility condition a₁!⋯aₖ! | n!), sumExcess (a₁+⋯+aₖ - n), and gExcess (the supremum g_k(n)). The two main conjectures ErdosProblem400a (average growth) and ErdosProblem400b (concentration) are stated using asymptotic notation. The Erdős-Graham upper bound g_k(n) ≤ C·log n is axiomatized. We prove non-negativity of g_k(n) and develop the k = 2 special case with its binomial coefficient interpretation.
keyInsights: **Multinomial Connection**: The condition a₁!⋯aₖ! | n! is equivalent to n!/(a₁!⋯aₖ!) being a (generalized) multinomial coefficient
**Logarithmic Bound**: Erdős-Graham proved g_k(n) = O(log n) by analyzing prime factorization constraints on the multinomial
**Two-Part Conjecture**: Part (a) asks about average behavior, part (b) about concentration — the latter is stronger and implies the former
**k = 2 Case**: Reduces to maximizing a + b - n with a!·b! | n!, intimately connected to binomial coefficients C(a+b, a)
**Precise Constants**: The conjectured constants cₖ depend on k and encode subtle information about the distribution of factorial divisibility

sections.title: Factorial Divisibility Condition
sections.summary: Defines FactorialDivides: the product ∏ aᵢ! divides n!.

sections.title: The Excess Function g_k
sections.summary: Defines sumExcess (sum minus n) and gExcess g_k(n) as the supremum of sum excesses.

sections.title: The Conjectures
sections.summary: States ErdosProblem400a (average growth ~ cₖ·x·log x), ErdosProblem400b (concentration), and combined ErdosProblem400.

sections.title: Known Upper Bound
sections.summary: Erdős-Graham upper bound: g_k(n) ≤ C·log n for all n.

sections.title: Basic Properties
sections.summary: Non-negativity of g_k(n) (since aᵢ = n, others = 0 gives excess 0) and binomial coefficient connection.

sections.title: The k = 2 Case
sections.summary: Characterization of the excess for k = 2 via binomial coefficients and the conjectured constant c₂.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #400 asks for precise asymptotics of g_k(n), the maximum sum excess under factorial divisibility. The Erdős-Graham upper bound O(log n) establishes the right order of magnitude, but the exact constants cₖ and concentration behavior remain open.
conclusion.implications: Understanding g_k(n) would reveal the fine structure of factorial divisibility and multinomial coefficients, connecting combinatorial number theory to the distribution of prime factors in factorials.
openQuestions: Does the average Σ g_k(n) / (x log x) converge to a constant cₖ?
Is g_k(n) concentrated around its mean for almost all n?
What is the exact value of c₂ for the k = 2 case?
How do the constants cₖ behave as k → ∞?
Is there a connection to the Stirling approximation or to p-adic valuations of multinomials?
